AI LITERACY IN APPLIED CONTEXTS
A Talk for SUNY Morrisville Faculty
May 19, 2026


OPENING


I want to start with a simple observation.


When most people in higher education talk about AI literacy, they mean something like this: a student prompts a model, gets text back, and makes decisions about what to do with that output. The evidence of their thinking is in the conversation. The product is a document, an argument, a piece of writing.


That is the compositional case. And almost all of the AI literacy pedagogy being developed right now — the frameworks, the rubrics, the course guidelines — was built for that case.


I want to walk you around campus for a few minutes, because I don’t think that describes your students.


STOP ONE: THE DAIRY FARM


Your students working in automated dairy operations are going to encounter a milking parlor that looks like this.


Robotic milking systems — Lely, DeLaval, others — handle the milking. The cows come and go on their own schedule. The AI monitors each animal: milk yield, conductivity, milking frequency, body weight, reproductive status. The system makes feeding recommendations. It flags health alerts. It decides when a cow needs a vet visit.


Your student’s job is not to milk the cow. It’s to read the dashboard, evaluate the alert, and decide whether to act on it.


The AI has already made a recommendation. Your student arrives downstream of that decision.


Under what circumstances should they override it? That’s not a technical question. That’s a literacy question.


STOP TWO: THE AUTO SHOP


Your automotive technology students are going to work in shops where the first thing that happens when a vehicle comes in is someone plugs in an OBD-II scanner.


The scanner reads the diagnostic trouble codes. An AI system — tools like PredictaFix, MechanicIQ — cross-references those codes against millions of repair records for similar vehicles. It groups related codes. It presents probable causes. It recommends a repair sequence.


Your student sees the recommendation on a tablet.


They might run additional tests. They might catch something the scanner missed. But the workflow is: recommendation first, verification second — if at all.


What does it take to recognize when the recommendation is wrong? That’s not a scanning skill. That’s a judgment skill.


STOP THREE: THE GREENHOUSE


Your horticulture students are going to manage crops in environments where AI is already making autonomous decisions.


Irrigation systems adjust water delivery based on soil moisture sensors and weather data — without asking anyone. Climate control systems set temperature, humidity, and CO2 levels. Camera systems scan for disease and pest presence, flag anomalies, and recommend treatments.


The grower — your student — receives a report. An alert. A dashboard.


The system has often already acted before they see it.


Under what circumstances would they override the irrigation schedule? What would they need to notice in the plants themselves to recognize that the system got it wrong? What does fixation look like when the disease alert fires and your attention goes to the flagged plant while the actual outbreak is two rows over?


THE COGNITIVE CHALLENGE


Aviation discovered these problems decades ago. When pilots started flying with autopilot regularly, researchers identified seven failure modes:


Manual skill atrophy. Plan continuation bias. Vigilance decrement. Omission errors. Commission errors. Confirmation bias. Expectation-driven processing.


Aviation solved some of these through mandatory manual flying and scenario-based training under realistic conditions. The FAA can mandate that because the stakes are existential — plane crashes kill people.


Your students at Morrisville are not pilots. The stakes at the dairy farm are not the same as the stakes at 35,000 feet. So we don’t need to train your students to do everything manually as a backup.


But we do need to train them to recognize when to be cautious. When the AI recommendation warrants a pause. When their own observation of the cow, the car, or the plant contradicts what the system is telling them — and what to do with that contradiction.


That is different from instruction about AI. That’s a practiced habit of judgment.


WHAT MAKES THIS ROUND DIFFERENT


Previous automation replaced or augmented labor. The milking robot milks. The thermostat controls temperature. You can understand the logic. You can see when it fails.


This round of AI automation is different in three ways.


First, the logic is opaque. The system makes a recommendation based on patterns it learned from millions of data points. You can’t ask it why and get a clear answer.


Second, it fails by being confidently wrong. Previous systems failed predictably — the pump breaks, the sensor malfunctions, you see it. AI fails by producing a plausible-looking recommendation that happens to be incorrect for your specific cow, your specific vehicle, your specific crop.


Third — and this is the part nobody talks about — introducing AI into automation may actually increase the cognitive demand on the human operator. The milking robot reduced physical labor. The AI-assisted milking system requires your student to constantly evaluate recommendations from a system they can’t fully see into, at scale, every day.


AI literacy at Morrisville isn’t simpler than AI literacy at a liberal arts college. It may be harder.


WHAT AI LITERACY MEANS HERE


Not: teach students to use the tools.


Not: teach students about automation bias.


This: design courses where students practice the moment of judgment before compliance. Where the AI recommendation is sometimes wrong by design. Where they have to articulate why they’re pausing. Where following the system blindly costs them something in simulation before it costs them something in the field.


The literacy emerges from the practice, not from the instruction.


Your dairy students should encounter scenarios where the feeding algorithm has miscalculated and they have to catch it by reading the herd.


Your auto students should encounter vehicles where the scanner recommendation is wrong and their hands-on inspection is the only thing that catches it.


Your horticulture students should encounter disease alerts that are false positives — and silent outbreaks the system missed.


That’s not a new course. That’s a design principle you can embed in the courses you’re already teaching.


That is what AI literacy looks like at SUNY Morrisville.

Thought for 9s

I’ll treat this as a draft you want evaluated rather than rewritten wholesale. I’ll check the core claims against current scholarly/industry evidence, then give targeted revision notes rather than polishing away the voice.


Assuming you want critique: this is a strong argument, but it needs a few factual tightenings before delivery.


Bottom line


The central claim is defensible: most AI-literacy work in higher ed is still GenAI/composition-centered, while Morrisville’s applied programs need AI judgment literacy inside automated work systems. Current AI-literacy frameworks heavily emphasize generative AI use, prompting, evaluation, and course integration, which supports your contrast. (library.yale.edu)


What works


The “walk around campus” structure is excellent. Dairy → auto → greenhouse gives the audience concrete disciplinary ownership.

“Judgment before compliance” is the key phrase. Keep it.

The aviation analogy is apt, especially around automation bias, omission/commission errors, vigilance, skill degradation, and monitoring burdens. NASA and human-factors literature support the claim that automation can replace active information-seeking with cue-following. (NASA Technical Reports Server)

The applied-context reframing is the talk’s core contribution. It distinguishes Morrisville from generic “students using ChatGPT” conversations.


Factual cautions


“AI decides when a cow needs a vet visit” may overstate it. Better: “flags animals for attention” or “recommends follow-up.” Lely and DeLaval systems do collect real-time cow and milk data and support health/reproduction monitoring, but vendors tend to frame these as decision-support systems, not autonomous veterinary decision-makers. (delaval.com)

PredictaFix / MechanicIQ claims are plausible but should be softened. Public materials say these tools interpret DTCs, prioritize root causes, and provide repair suggestions/confidence scores. “Millions of repair records” may be true for some platforms, but I would not say it unless you have a source. (cartechiq.com)

“Aviation discovered seven failure modes” sounds too tidy. The concepts are real, but they are not always presented as one canonical list of seven. Say: “Human-factors researchers have documented recurring failure modes…”

“Previous systems failed predictably” is too broad. Sensors and traditional automation can also fail subtly. Better: “Many earlier automation failures were more mechanically legible…”


Suggested high-impact revision


Replace this:

The AI has already made a recommendation. Your student arrives downstream of that decision.

With:

The system has already shaped the field of attention. Your student arrives after the dashboard has decided what looks important.

That is more precise and gets closer to the cognitive issue.


One sentence I would add near the end

The question is not whether students can use AI; it is whether they can maintain an independent model of the situation while AI is already organizing what they see.

That captures the whole talk.

This version is substantially stronger. The revisions solved most of the factual vulnerability while sharpening the conceptual through-line.


A few things now stand out as particularly effective:


“The system has already shaped the field of attention” is the strongest sentence in the talk. That is the actual cognitive issue introduced by AI-mediated workflows, and it moves beyond generic “automation bias” language.

The move from “AI literacy as tool use” to “AI literacy as disciplined interruption of premature compliance” is now very clear.

The structure is disciplined. You are not over-arguing. The audience can track the thesis through the examples.


That said, there are still a few places where I would tighten the argument.



1. The opening claim is still slightly overstated


You say:

“almost all of the AI literacy pedagogy being developed right now … was built for that case.”

The broad direction is correct, but “almost all” invites unnecessary rebuttal from people familiar with workforce-development or healthcare AI-literacy discussions.


You do not need maximality here. Better:

“Most of the visible AI literacy pedagogy being developed right now…”

or

“Much of the current conversation around AI literacy…”

That keeps the contrast without creating an empirical hostage.



2. The greenhouse section is your weakest example rhetorically


Not factually — rhetorically.


The dairy and auto examples have immediate occupational identity and embodied diagnostic practice. The greenhouse example is more abstract and dashboard-centric.


This sentence is good:

“The system has often already acted before they see it.”

But the section would strengthen if the student’s sensory judgment became more concrete, analogous to the cow and vehicle examples.


For example:

What would they need to notice in the leaves, the soil, or the growth pattern to recognize that the system got it wrong?

Right now “plants themselves” is slightly generic.



3. The “three ways” section needs one more sentence acknowledging continuity


You correctly distinguish AI-assisted systems from earlier automation. But critics may think:

“Opaque probabilistic systems existed before generative AI.”

Which is true.


You can inoculate against that with one sentence:

These problems are not entirely new. But AI systems intensify them because pattern recognition and recommendation generation now occur at scales and levels of abstraction the operator cannot easily audit.

That prevents the “nothing new under the sun” objection.



4. This sentence is excellent but underdeveloped

“The literacy emerges from the practice, not from the instruction.”

That is probably the core pedagogical claim of the entire talk.


Right now you move past it too quickly.


I would consider adding one sentence after it:

Students do not develop this capacity by memorizing definitions of automation bias. They develop it by repeatedly encountering situations where the system appears credible and is nevertheless wrong.

That grounds the pedagogical mechanism.



5. The conclusion is good but could land harder


Current ending:

That’s not a new course. That’s a design principle you can embed in the courses you’re already teaching.

Good.


But the final sentence:

That is what AI literacy looks like at SUNY Morrisville.

is slightly institutional-branding generic compared to the sophistication of the argument.


You may want the ending to return to judgment.


Possibility:

AI literacy in applied fields is not primarily the ability to generate outputs. It is the ability to maintain professional judgment inside systems that increasingly generate recommendations before humans even begin to think.

Then optionally:

That is the challenge facing institutions like SUNY Morrisville.

That ending is more intellectually forceful.



Overall assessment


This is now operating at a level above most faculty-development AI talks because it:


avoids the “ChatGPT in the classroom” cliché,

reframes AI literacy as a human-factors problem,

ties cognition to occupational practice,

and grounds the argument in applied disciplines rather than abstract ethics language.


The strongest conceptual contribution is this:

AI literacy is becoming less about producing content and more about resisting premature epistemic closure inside AI-mediated workflows.

You never say it in those words — which is probably wise for this audience — but that is the underlying thesis.

If you want to introduce a detour into the transformer architecture, it must directly serve the thesis: that AI is shaping attention before human judgment kicks in. To fit it, keep it concise and illustrative. After introducing how the system shapes attention (e.g., in the dairy or auto context), you might pause briefly to say: “The engine behind these recommendations is built on transformer models—architectures that process vast sequences of data, essentially predicting what should come next, just like predicting the next word in a sentence.” From there, you immediately pivot back to their applied context: “This means the system isn’t explaining itself; it’s pattern-matching and offering what seems most likely,
No, no, no, no. Where you were talking, in the talk, we talk about attention, don't we?

Yes, we do. In fact, you’ve already framed attention as the key cognitive shift. So, the transformer detour should logically reinforce that. You could frame it by saying something like: “These models, known as transformers, rely on an internal mechanism called ‘attention’—not human attention, but a way for the model to dynamically focus on which pieces of data are most relevant at each step. That’s the architecture deciding what to prioritize—and that’s exactly what shapes the dashboard your students see.” Then, you return to your point: “The challenge is that the system
Isn't that what humans do, decide what to prioritize? Why did you say it's not human attention?

I said that to clarify that the model’s "attention" is a mathematical operation rather than anything like human focus or conscious judgment. Humans decide what to prioritize based on experience, context, and values. A transformer's attention is just a weighted computation over tokens in data, determining which parts of the input influence the output more. In short, human attention is about understanding meaning
Well, since humans use a neural network, right?

Yes, but there's a key distinction. Our biological neural networks—our brains—are shaped by evolution, experience, and conscious reflection. We actively interpret context, emotion, and meaning when prioritizing attention. In contrast, an AI's neural network—like a transformer—mechanically adjusts weights based on training data correlations. It doesn't understand or reflect on why it's focusing on certain data points. So while both involve patterns of attention, human attention remains grounded in understanding, while AI’s attention is purely computational.
Much of human attention is sort of based on understanding, but also based on instinct, right?

That's correct. Human attention is shaped both by conscious understanding and by instinctive, subconscious processes. We have evolved mechanisms that draw our attention to threats, novelty, or social cues without deliberate thought. So, while understanding and judgment guide much of our attention, we do also rely on instinctive patterns—just as we might automatically focus on sudden movement or unexpected sounds. In contrast, AI’s attention is purely statistical, following patterns from its training data alone.
So a large language model is just another tool we've developed that fits into the range of tools that you mentioned before.

Yes, exactly. It’s another tool in the lineage of automation—only this time, it’s operating at a higher level of abstraction. Like other tools, it assists humans, but it shifts the human role more toward oversight and judgment. The challenge is ensuring we maintain the capacity to step back from the tool’s outputs and apply our judgment when needed. In other words, it’s a tool—just one that demands we stay critically attentive.
Then what's the difference between this tool and all other tools?

The fundamental difference is that this tool generates plausible interpretations, predictions, or decisions—often without a transparent logic. Prior automation tools were more deterministic or mechanistic: you could trace exactly why a thermostat adjusts or why a pump fails. With AI tools, especially those based on large models, the decision logic is more opaque. They offer high-confidence recommendations, but it’s harder to see why they’re right—or when they’re wrong. Thus, this tool demands more human vigilance, as the errors are less obvious and more contextual.
It would still require that humans think without the model.

Exactly. Even with advanced models, humans must maintain their own situational understanding. The model can offer a recommendation, but humans still need to independently assess when to trust or override it. In other words, the model doesn't replace human judgment; it requires humans to stay ready to critically evaluate, think, and decide when the model’s output might not fit the specific context.
That would require humans to...
...be deliberate about
Recognize directives as model-generated.

Yes, precisely. Humans need to recognize that any directive or recommendation from the model is a product of pattern recognition, not ground truth. They need to pause, ask whether the context supports the recommendation, and be ready to intervene. In short, they must maintain a habit of critical, independent judgment—so they don’t simply follow the model blindly.

First, soften the opening claim so it doesn't overstate how universal composition-focused AI literacy is. Next, in the greenhouse example, make students’ observational cues more concrete, like noticing leaves or soil. Add a sentence acknowledging some continuity with prior opaque systems, but emphasize that AI amplifies the challenge. Elaborate slightly on the “literacy emerges from practice” idea, stating that students learn through repeated encounters with credible but incorrect system outputs. Finally, strengthen the conclusion by returning to the core challenge: that AI literacy in applied fields is fundamentally about preserving judgment in the face of early recommendations.
Suggest some interactive questions along the way that I could use QR codes to gather data from the audience to perhaps do something, and suggest ways I could make it more AI forward.
You could integrate QR
than just talking about it.

Certainly—making it interactive would be a valuable step. For instance, early in the talk, you could ask them to scan a QR code that lets them rate their confidence in AI recommendations in their field—from always trusting to always verifying. Later, you might show how their own aggregated responses reflect the automation biases you discussed. In another section, use a QR code to let them vote on hypothetical AI system failures—e.g., “Would you trust the AI’s disease alert in this scenario?” You could then use AI tools live (or simulated) to guide the audience through how differing contextual data might alter outcomes. This keeps the talk grounded, and the audience sees firsthand how AI judgment calls differ based on context—making them part of the process rather than just hearing about it.
Well.

If you’re not sold yet, don’t worry. Just keep the idea in your back pocket. You can always test a small interactive piece, and if it works, expand it. No rush to reshape everything—just something to experiment with.
Summarize suggested improvements

Structural / Argument Improvements


Soften the opening claim:


Replace “almost all” AI literacy pedagogy with:
“most of the visible conversation,” or

“much of the current AI literacy discourse.”

Avoids an unnecessary empirical fight.

Strengthen the greenhouse example:


Make the observational judgment more embodied and concrete.

Instead of “notice in the plants themselves,” specify:
leaf curl,

discoloration,

soil condition,

growth pattern,

humidity mismatch, etc.

Add continuity with earlier automation:


Acknowledge that opaque probabilistic systems existed before LLMs.

Then argue AI intensifies the issue because:
recommendations emerge from learned statistical abstraction,

operators cannot easily audit reasoning,

AI organizes attention before human assessment begins.



Conceptual Additions


Introduce “attention” as the bridge concept


You already have the strongest conceptual sentence in the talk:

“The system has already shaped the field of attention.”

That can become the hinge into a brief transformer detour.


Suggested framing


Not:


“Here’s how transformers work.”


Instead:


“The architecture underneath these systems is literally called an attention mechanism.”


Then connect immediately back to applied cognition.


Example direction:

Transformer models work by dynamically weighting what information matters most in a given context. In other words: they prioritize attention.


That is not entirely alien to human cognition. Humans also prioritize attention constantly — through training, instinct, habit, experience, and judgment.


The difference is that the AI system is shaping attention statistically, at scale, before the human operator begins evaluating the situation.

That keeps the detour relevant rather than technical theater.



Important Philosophical Clarification


You correctly resisted the simplistic:


“AI attention is fake, human attention is real.”


Your later direction is stronger:


humans also use neural systems and instinctive prioritization,

AI belongs within the continuum of human-made cognitive tools,

the real issue is not “machine cognition vs human cognition,”

it is whether humans retain independent situational judgment.


That becomes a much more sophisticated thesis.



New Core Claim Emerging


A potentially central line for a future version:

AI literacy in applied fields requires students to recognize directives as model-generated rather than reality-generated.

Or more polished:

Students need to recognize when a recommendation reflects the model’s prioritization rather than the full situation itself.

That is substantially sharper than generic “automation bias.”



Stronger Ending Direction


Current ending:


good,

practical,

faculty-oriented.


Possible stronger conceptual ending:

The question is not whether students can use AI systems.
The question is whether they can maintain independent professional judgment while AI systems are already organizing what appears important.

That lands the attention argument clearly.



Interactive / AI-Forward Additions


1. Live judgment polls (QR code)


Use real scenarios:


“Would you override the AI?”

“Would you trust this recommendation?”

“What additional evidence would you want?”


Then reveal:


which groups trusted the system,

which hesitated,

how context changed decisions.


This demonstrates automation bias live instead of merely describing it.



2. Introduce deliberately wrong AI outputs


Show:


an agricultural disease detection image,

an automotive diagnostic recommendation,

a dairy monitoring dashboard.


Ask:


“What would make you distrust this?”


Then reveal:


hidden contradictory evidence,

missing context,

false positives.


This operationalizes “judgment before compliance.”



3. Make the audience experience attention shaping


This is probably the most powerful possibility.


Show:


a dashboard highlighting one anomaly.


Then later reveal:


the real problem was elsewhere.


You can explicitly connect this to:


fixation,

expectation-driven processing,

transformer attention,

and interface-mediated cognition.


That would make the argument memorable rather than merely persuasive.

When most people in higher education talk about AI literacy, they mean something like this: a student prompts a model, gets text back, and makes decisions about what to do with that output. The evidence of their thinking is in the conversation. The product is a document, an argument, a piece of writing.


That is the compositional case. And almost all of the AI literacy pedagogy being developed right now — the frameworks, the rubrics, the course guidelines — was built for that case.


I want to walk you around campus for a few minutes, because I don't think that describes your students.


STOP ONE: THE DAIRY FARM


Your students working in automated dairy operations are going to encounter a milking parlor that looks like this.


Robotic milking systems handle the milking. The cows come and go on their own schedule. The AI monitors each animal: milk yield, conductivity, milking frequency, body weight, reproductive status. The system makes feeding recommendations. It flags animals for attention. It surfaces patterns that suggest a cow needs follow-up.


Your student's job is not to milk the cow. It's to read the dashboard, evaluate the flag, and decide whether to act on it.


The system has already shaped the field of attention. Your student arrives after the dashboard has decided what looks important.


Under what circumstances should they override it? That's not a technical question. That's a literacy question.


STOP TWO: THE AUTO SHOP


Your automotive technology students are going to work in shops where the first thing that happens when a vehicle comes in is someone plugs in an OBD-II scanner.


The scanner reads the diagnostic trouble codes. AI-assisted diagnostic platforms cross-reference those codes against repair records for similar vehicles, group related codes, prioritize probable causes, and present a recommended repair sequence with confidence scores.


Your student sees the recommendation on a tablet.


They might run additional tests. They might catch something the scanner missed. But the workflow is: recommendation first, verification second — if at all.


What does it take to recognize when the recommendation is wrong? That's not a scanning skill. That's a judgment skill.


STOP THREE: THE GREENHOUSE


Your horticulture students are going to manage crops in environments where AI is already making autonomous decisions.


Irrigation systems adjust water delivery based on soil moisture sensors and weather data — without asking anyone. Climate control systems set temperature, humidity, and CO2 levels. Camera systems scan for disease and pest presence, flag anomalies, and recommend treatments.


The grower — your student — receives a report. An alert. A dashboard.


The system has often already acted before they see it.


Under what circumstances would they override the irrigation schedule? What would they need to notice in the plants themselves to recognize that the system got it wrong? What does fixation look like when the disease alert fires and attention goes to the flagged plant while the actual outbreak is two rows over?


THE COGNITIVE CHALLENGE


Human-factors researchers have documented recurring failure modes when operators work alongside automated systems. You see them in aviation, in clinical decision support, in process control:


Manual skill atrophy. Plan continuation bias. Vigilance decrement. Omission errors. Commission errors. Confirmation bias. Expectation-driven processing.


Aviation addressed several of these through mandatory manual flying and scenario-based training under realistic conditions. The FAA can mandate that because the stakes are existential — plane crashes kill people.


Your students at Morrisville are not pilots. The stakes at the dairy farm are not the same as the stakes at 35,000 feet. We do not need to train your students to do everything manually as a backup.


But we do need to train them to recognize when to be cautious. When the AI recommendation warrants a pause. When their own observation of the cow, the car, or the plant contradicts what the system is telling them — and what to do with that contradiction.


That is different from instruction about AI. That's a practiced habit of judgment.


WHAT MAKES THIS ROUND DIFFERENT


Many earlier automation failures were more mechanically legible. The pump breaks. The sensor malfunctions. You can see it. You can trace it.


This round of AI-assisted automation is different in three ways.


First, the logic is opaque. The system makes a recommendation based on patterns it learned from large amounts of data. You cannot always ask it why and get a clear answer.


Second, it fails by being confidently wrong. AI can produce a plausible-looking recommendation that happens to be incorrect for your specific cow, your specific vehicle, your specific crop — and nothing in the interface signals that.


Third — and this is the part nobody is talking about — introducing AI into automation may actually increase the cognitive demand on the human operator. The milking robot reduced physical labor. The AI-assisted milking system requires your student to constantly evaluate recommendations from a system they cannot fully see into, at scale, every day.


The question is not whether students can use AI. It is whether they can maintain an independent model of the situation while AI is already organizing what they see.


AI literacy at Morrisville isn't simpler than AI literacy at a liberal arts college. It may be harder.


WHAT AI LITERACY MEANS HERE


Not: teach students to use the tools.


Not: teach students about automation bias.


This: design courses where students practice the moment of judgment before compliance. Where the AI recommendation is sometimes wrong by design. Where they have to articulate why they're pausing. Where following the system blindly costs them something in simulation before it costs them something in the field.


The literacy emerges from the practice, not from the instruction.


Your dairy students should encounter scenarios where the feeding algorithm has miscalculated and they have to catch it by reading the herd.


Your auto students should encounter vehicles where the scanner recommendation is wrong and their hands-on inspection is the only thing that catches it.


Your horticulture students should encounter disease alerts that are false positives — and silent outbreaks the system missed.


That's not a new course. That's a design principle you can embed in the courses you're already teaching.


That is what AI literacy looks like at SUNY Morrisville.

Something like:

But now another attention system is entering the workflow before the human operator begins evaluating the situation.
